items.applies_to: All apps whose rebuild fails at launch
items.maps_to: HackTricks smali-changes.md; sec-88 "Signing the APK"; MASTG-TECH-0039 (Repackaging & Re-Signing)
items.test: When repackaging breaks the app, find the signer-verification routine and patch the **final branch**, not the whole routine.
items.how:
Grep the smali tree and jadx output for the recognisable ingredients, then patch the last comparison before the error dialog / `finish()` / `System.exit()` / telemetry call:
```bash
grep -rnE 'GET_SIGNATURES|GET_SIGNING_CERTIFICATES|apkContentsSigners|MessageDigest|"SHA-256"|Base64|getInstallerPackageName|com\.android\.vending' $DEC/apktool/smali*/ $DEC/jadx/sources/
```
```smali
# force valid
const/4 v0, 0x1
# or invert the branch into the tamper handler
if-eqz v0, :tamper_detected   # original
if-nez v0, :tamper_detected   # patched
```
Smali gotchas that break rebuilds: raise `.locals`, **not** `.registers` (parameter registers `p0..pN` map to the highest registers); `move-result*` must immediately follow its `invoke-*`; `long`/`double` consume a register pair; use `invoke-*/range` for many or high-numbered registers. Forgetting a `.locals` increment produces a verifier crash at launch — the usual failure mode.
items.proof: The rebuilt APK survives launch and reaches the gated feature; logcat no longer shows the tamper path.
items.escalation: Unblocks D02-022; also worth checking the `getInstallerPackageName` gate (D02-020) first, which is often the cheaper patch.
items.ruled_out_when: No signer-check ingredients appear in the decompiled tree, or the check is server-side (D02-024), in which case local patching cannot help and you must re-scope.

items.title: Server-verified attestation: stop, and re-scope
items.applies_to: Any app calling Play Integrity, a residual SafetyNet path, or a commercial RASP SDK with a server-side verdict check
items.maps_to: Local corpus ref 18 §L, ref 24 §A4.7; Play Integrity device labels `MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY` / `MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY` / `MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY` / `MEETS_VIRTUAL_INTEGRITY`
items.test: Before repacking, establish whether the integrity gate is local (hookable, patchable) or a **server-verified attestation** (not defeatable by any local hook). Getting this wrong costs hours.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'SafetyNet|IntegrityManager|IntegrityTokenRequest|attest|StandardIntegrityManager' $DEC/jadx/sources/
grep -rnE 'getInstallerPackageName|getInstallSourceInfo|GET_SIGNING_CERTIFICATES' $DEC/jadx/sources/
adb logcat -d | grep -iE 'integrity|deviceRecognitionVerdict|MEETS_(DEVICE|BASIC|STRONG|VIRTUAL)_INTEGRITY|attest|rasp|rooted'
```
Then look at the wire: does a token go to the client's own backend, and does the response differ when the device is rooted/emulated?
items.proof: The network request carrying the attestation token, and a materially different server response on an uncertified device. That is the attestation being *enforced*; if the response is identical, the attestation is decorative and belongs in D02-021.
items.escalation: If enforced, the D21 RASP surface is closed to instrumentation — re-scope to server-side testing (D15) rather than burning hours on Frida. If decorative, file per D02-021 and proceed with D02-022.
items.ruled_out_when: No attestation SDK is present, **or** the verdict is evaluated client-side only (you can see the branch in jadx and hook it), **or** the server response is byte-identical with and without a valid token.

items.title: Custom APK verifier confusion: v3→v2 fallback and the unvalidated content digest
items.vrt: `cryptographic_weakness.insufficient_verification_of_data_authenticity.cryptographic_signature` (varies) -> `server_side_injection.remote_code_execution_rce` (P1) equivalent impact when the target installs arbitrary apps under a trusted signer allowlist
items.attacker: AM-03 zero-permission local app (places the artefact) / AM-09 (supplies it over the network)
items.applies_to: OEM app stores, plugin managers, enterprise/MDM installers, in-app updaters — any code path enforcing its **own** signer allowlist before handing a file to `PackageInstaller`
items.maps_to: HackTricks android-applications-basics.md ("Custom APK verifier confusion / mixed-scheme abuse"); the Samsung Galaxy Store / S25 five-bug chain (bugscale); MASWE-0011
items.test: Stores, updaters, plugin managers and enterprise installers that run their own signature check frequently disagree with the platform. Two classic errors: (a) falling back to v2 when a present v3 block fails signer validation; (b) verifying that the signature *over the embedded digest* is valid without recomputing the digest from the APK contents. The Samsung chain had both — "it checks that the signature over the digest present in the signature block is valid, but it does not check that the APK data hashes to the same digest."
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'ApkSignatureSchemeV2Verifier|ApkSigningBlock|APK Sig Block 42|GET_SIGNATURES|GET_SIGNING_CERTIFICATES|verifySignature|MessageDigest' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | grep -v android/support
# build a payload with the expected package name, sign v3-only with your key
apksigner sign --ks key.jks --out payload-v3.apk \
  --v1-signing-enabled false --v2-signing-enabled false --v3-signing-enabled true payload.apk
apksigner verify --verbose --print-certs payload-v3.apk
# transplant a trusted APK's v2 signing block onto the payload (graft_sig.py-style)
```
Red flags in the verifier code: a v2 fallback on v3 signer-validation failure; a v2 check that never recomputes the content digest; package-name or metadata checks not bound to the file body.
items.proof: The target's own verifier accepts the grafted APK — its "valid signature" log line or dialog fires and the install proceeds — while `apksigner verify --print-certs` on the *same file* shows **your** v3 certificate.
items.escalation: Pair with D02-026 to land the file where the updater picks it up without user confirmation, and with a D07 path-traversal write to place it (the bugscale chain wrote to `/data/data/com.sec.android.app.samsungapps/files/samsungapps-<productID>-<fileSize>-<versionCode>`).
items.ruled_out_when: The app hands the file straight to `PackageInstaller` with no verification of its own (then the platform's verifier is authoritative and this item does not apply — go to D02-027), **or** the verifier recomputes the content digest from the APK bytes and compares it to the signed digest, **or** it rejects on any v3 signer-validation failure without falling back.

items.title: Deterministic installer cache: artefact substitution before install
items.severity_note: High — Critical when the flow auto-installs helper APKs or plugins without user confirmation
items.vrt: `insecure_data_transport.executable_download.no_secure_integrity_check` (P4) as the baseline, overridden upward by the demonstrated install
items.attacker: AM-03 zero-permission local app (writing to a shared path) or AM-04 with legacy storage access
items.applies_to: Apps with a self-update, plugin, or "shell APK" install path
items.maps_to: HackTricks android-applications-basics.md ("Deterministic installer cache / artifact substitution")
items.test: If a store, updater or helper downloads an installable artefact to a **deterministic path** and decides "already downloaded" from existence plus size only (e.g. `file.length() >= expectedSize`), writing attacker bytes to that exact path makes the next trigger install your artefact.
items.how:
Find the destination in jadx (look for a path built from productID/size/versionCode), then:
```bash
adb shell run-as com.target sh -c 'ls -l files/ cache/ no_backup/ 2>/dev/null'
adb shell ls -l /sdcard/Android/data/com.target/cache/          # externally writable staging
# place the payload at the exact path and pad to >= expectedSize, then fire the trigger
adb shell 'cat /sdcard/payload.apk > /sdcard/Android/data/com.target/cache/<exact-name>'
adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "<trigger deep link>"
```
items.proof: The install flow proceeds **without re-downloading** and installs your APK/plugin; `pm list packages -i` shows the target app recorded as the installer of a package you supplied.
items.escalation: Pair with D02-025 to also pass the app's custom signer check; -> D07 if the write primitive is a FileProvider path traversal rather than a shared directory.
items.ruled_out_when: The destination path incorporates a server-supplied nonce or content hash, **or** the app verifies the downloaded file's digest against a server-supplied value before install, **or** the staging directory is app-private and no write primitive reaches it (prove that by attempting the write as a zero-permission app, not by reading the manifest).

items.title: Self-hosted / side-loaded update channel without pinned signature verification
items.vrt: `insecure_data_transport.executable_download.no_secure_integrity_check` (P4 baseline, CWE-494) — override upward with the code-execution proof; `insecure_os_firmware.weakness_in_firmware_updates.firmware_does_not_validate_update_integrity` (P3) for device/OEM scope
items.attacker: AM-09 malicious backend/CDN; AM-06 network attacker if the fetch is cleartext or unpinned
items.applies_to: All apps with an out-of-Play update path (enterprise, regional, OEM). On `targetSdk >= 26` the installer requires `REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES`. ATT&CK M1006 covers `exec()` only: the API 29+ W^X change stops executing a *file* from internal data storage, not `System.load()`/`dlopen()` of a `.so` nor a `DexClassLoader` on a DEX/JAR — every second stage (native, DEX, JS) remains fully current (D02-042).
items.maps_to: ATT&CK T1407 Download New Code at Runtime, T1661 Application Versioning ("An adversary may push an update to a previously benign application to add malicious code"; SharkBot S1055), T1544 Ingress Tool Transfer, mitigation M1006; MASWE-0049 (CWE-494); MASVS-CODE-3
items.test: Can the app fetch and run code after install — a DEX/JAR/SO/AAB fragment, a JS bundle, a plugin, a full APK? Then: is the artefact signature-verified against a **pinned** key, and is the fetch over pinned TLS?
items.proof: A packet capture showing the artefact fetched over a channel you control, plus the on-screen installer prompt for **your** package (screen recording of the client's own UI offering your APK is the deliverable), **or** for the loader variant a marker file written from inside the app's UID by your payload's static initialiser — use an 8+ character random marker (`/data/data/<pkg>/files/zq7k4mx2`), never `PWNED` or `test`, and confirm the marker string does not already occur anywhere in the baseline app.
items.escalation: RCE in the app UID gives you every local-storage, Keystore and session primitive at once — chain into D11, D12 and D13 and report as one Critical. -> D14 if the fetch is cleartext or MitM-able, which changes the attacker from a supply-chain insider to any hostile network. -> D24 if the URL arrives in a push payload; -> D09 if it arrives in a deep link.
items.ruled_out_when: No dynamic-load or install call site exists in the shipped code, **or** the downloaded artefact's signature is verified against a key pinned in the app (show the verification code and that it fails closed on a substituted file), **or** the fetch is certificate-pinned *and* the artefact is signed *and* the load path is a read-only app-private file. Absence of a `REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES` permission rules out the APK-install variant but **not** the DEX/JS variant.

items.title: The app enables unknown-sources installation or installs other packages
items.severity_note: High — Critical if the install is silent (device owner) or the URL is fetched over cleartext/unpinned TLS
items.vrt: `insecure_data_transport.executable_download.no_secure_integrity_check` (P4) with an upward override on the demonstrated install
items.attacker: AM-02 remote one click (the user accepts a prompt from a trusted app) / AM-09
items.applies_to: All. `REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES` is per-app from **Android 8**; before that a single global "unknown sources" toggle applied — **LEGACY**.
items.maps_to: ATT&CK T1632.001 Code Signing Policy Modification (Dvmap, Mandrake "can enable app installation from unknown sources"), T1544, T1632; mitigations M1006, M1011, M1012
items.test: Does the app hold `REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES`, drive the user to the unknown-sources settings screen, or call `PackageInstaller`? An app that can install other APKs is a distribution channel; if the APK URL is attacker-influenceable it is a malware-delivery vector wearing the client's brand.
items.how:
```bash
aapt2 dump permissions base.apk | grep -E 'REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES|INSTALL_PACKAGES|DELETE_PACKAGES'
grep -rnE 'PackageInstaller|ACTION_INSTALL_PACKAGE|ACTION_MANAGE_UNKNOWN_APP_SOURCES|Settings\.ACTION_SECURITY_SETTINGS|setInstallerPackageName' $DEC/jadx/sources/
# where does the URL come from?
grep -rn -B4 -A4 '\.apk' $DEC/jadx/sources/ | grep -nE 'getString|Uri\.parse|intent\.getData|remoteConfig|fcm|payload'
```
items.proof: MitM the config or push that supplies the APK URL, substitute your own signed test APK, and record the client app launching the install prompt for **your** package.
items.escalation: -> D09 (a deep link that supplies the URL gives a one-click, no-permission-prompt chain from a web page to an install prompt); -> D24 (push-delivered URL); -> D18 (remote-config-delivered URL).
items.ruled_out_when: The permission is absent and no `PackageInstaller` call site exists, **or** the APK URL is a compile-time constant pointing at a pinned, certificate-verified host and the artefact's signature is checked before the install intent is raised. An SDK-contributed `REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES` (see D02-043) still counts — attribute it, do not dismiss it.

items.title: `android:debuggable="true"` in a release build → private-storage read on a stock device
items.vrt: The flag alone is `insecure_data_storage.sensitive_application_data_stored_unencrypted.on_internal_storage` (**P5**) — you override it with the reachability proof. The extracted credential routes to `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_publicly_accessible_asset` (P1) or `insecure_os_firmware.hardcoded_password.non_privileged_user` (P2) if static.
items.attacker: AM-03 zero-permission local app / AM-11 physical unlocked (anyone who picks up the phone with USB debugging on)
items.applies_to: All. Release builds default to `false`, so any `true` is an explicit build mistake.
items.maps_to: MASTG-TEST-0226 (Debuggable Flag Enabled in the AndroidManifest), MASWE-0063 (CWE-489), MASVS-RESILIENCE-4, MASTG-KNOW-0007, MASTG-TECH-0150, MASTG-TECH-0117; ATT&CK T1409 Stored Application Data, T1533, T1623.001; developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/risks/android-debuggable
items.test: Detect the flag three independent ways (a repacked or SDK-injected build can differ from what you expect), then **use it** — the flag is not the finding, the extracted credential is. MASTG itself links Android's note that the flag "is not considered a direct vulnerability"; do not hand a triager the flag.
items.how:
```bash
aapt2 dump badging base.apk | grep -i debuggable            # prints "application-debuggable"
adb shell dumpsys package com.target.app | grep -Ei 'flags=.*DEBUGGABLE|pkgFlags='
adb shell getprop ro.debuggable                             # 0 on a production device image
adb shell getprop ro.build.type                             # must read "user" for the claim to hold
# then actually use it, as a normal non-root shell:
adb shell run-as com.target.app id
adb shell run-as com.target.app ls -la /data/data/com.target.app/{shared_prefs,databases,files}
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell "run-as $PKG sh -c 'cat shared_prefs/*.xml'"      # the glob must expand INSIDE run-as; an unquoted host-side glob aborts zsh with 'no matches found'
```
drozer equivalent: `run app.package.debuggable -f com.target`.
items.proof: `run-as` returning `uid=10xxx(u0_aXXX)` and a directory listing of the private data dir on a **stock, non-rooted, production (`ro.build.type=user`)** device, with an actual bearer token / refresh token / PAN / password in the output. Then replay that token against the production API from your own machine and screenshot the 200 with victim data. `run-as` succeeding is the *operational* proof; the manifest flag and `dumpsys` line are only declarations.
items.escalation: The extracted token is the input to every D15 IDOR/BOLA test; a static credential becomes P1 if it authenticates to an internet-facing service. Also -> D02-030 (JDWP code execution), -> D02-031 (`adb backup` re-enabled), -> D11, -> D12, -> D13. Twin row: D03-071 — mark it from `logs/D02-029.txt`; do not re-run.
items.ruled_out_when: `aapt2 dump badging` prints no `application-debuggable` line **and** `adb shell run-as com.target.app id` fails with `run-as: package not debuggable` on a `ro.build.type=user` device. Both — a userdebug test image makes `run-as` succeed regardless of the app, which is a harness artefact, not a finding. Check every flavour and variant the client ships, not just the Play build.

items.title: Debuggable build → JDWP attach → arbitrary code in the app's UID
items.vrt: `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (P1) when the in-process execution mints or reads a live session; the primitive itself is rated by what it yields
items.applies_to: All debuggable builds, all API levels — this legacy check is fully alive
items.maps_to: MASTG-TECH-0031 (Debugging), MASTG-TECH-0040 (Waiting for the Debugger), MASTG-TOOL-0019 (jdb); drozer `app.package.debuggable`, `exploit.jdwp.check`
items.test: `android:debuggable="true"` allows a JDWP debugger to attach and execute arbitrary code **inside the app's process, with its UID and permissions** — no root, no Frida, no instrumentation the app can detect as instrumentation. This is the path when Frida is detected or the app crashes under hooking.
items.how:
```bash
adb jdwp                                  # the PID appears here only if debuggable
adb forward tcp:8700 jdwp:<pid>
jdb -attach localhost:8700
```
```
stop in com.target.app.security.BridgeGate.isAllowed
locals
print this.allowList
set this.allowList = "*"
```
drozer's `exploit.jdwp.check` states the mechanism verbatim: *"Open @jdwp-control and see which applications connect. This is an issue because then drozer can act as a debugger for the connected application. This could be used to invoke arbitrary code within the context of the debuggable application."*
items.proof: `jdb` breaking in the app's own classes and printing/modifying locals, plus the changed behaviour on screen. Screenshot the `adb jdwp` PID list and the `jdb` session together.
items.escalation: -> D12 (call the Keystore-backed decrypt routine **in-process**, defeating a "the key never leaves Keystore" design without extracting any key) -> D13 (read the session object directly) -> D10 (read exactly what a WebView allow-list compares).
items.ruled_out_when: The package's PID never appears in `adb jdwp` on a `ro.build.type=user` device. The `@jdwp-control` global path in drozer's `exploit.jdwp.check` is a legacy device-level check — on modern Android the per-app `debuggable` flag is the live vector, so a negative on the global check does not rule this out.

items.title: Debuggable re-enables `adb backup` at targetSdk 31+
items.vrt: `mobile_security_misconfiguration.auto_backup_allowed_by_default` (P5) for the flag; the extracted credential routes to `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.*` (P1–P3)
items.attacker: AM-11 physical unlocked with USB debugging; AM-03 where a local app can drive the backup
items.applies_to: `targetSdk >= 31` for the backup gate; `debuggable` matters on all versions. `allowBackup` defaults to **true** below targetSdk 31 where no `dataExtractionRules` is supplied — flag the default, not just an explicit `true`.
items.maps_to: developer.android.com/about/versions/12/behavior-changes-12 ("`adb backup` excludes app data for apps targeting Android 12; opt-in by setting `android:debuggable="true"`... Must set to false before release"); ATT&CK T1409, T1533
items.test: For `targetSdk >= 31`, `adb backup` excludes app data **unless** `android:debuggable="true"`. A release build carrying `debuggable="true"` therefore hands you a full data extraction with no root, on top of the usual debuggability impact.
items.how:
```bash
grep -oE 'android:(debuggable|allowBackup|fullBackupContent|dataExtractionRules)="[^"]*"' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
adb -s "$SERIAL" backup -f out.ab -noapk "$PKG" && ls -l out.ab            # accept the on-device prompt; a header-only file is ~1 KiB
head -c 24 out.ab | head -4                                                 # ANDROID BACKUP / 5 / 1=compressed / none=unencrypted
tail -c +25 out.ab | python3 -c 'import sys,zlib; sys.stdout.buffer.write(zlib.decompress(sys.stdin.buffer.read()))' > out.tar   # line 3 == 0: skip decompress; line 4 != none: AES — use `abe unpack out.ab out.tar <password>`
mkdir -p ab && tar -xf out.tar -C ab && find ab -type f | wc -l
grep -rniE 'token|session|bearer|password|refresh' "ab/apps/$PKG/sp" "ab/apps/$PKG/db" "ab/apps/$PKG/f" 2>/dev/null
```
items.proof: `application-debuggable` in badging output plus a non-trivially-sized `.ab` whose unpacked tar contains `shared_prefs/*.xml` with a live session token. Grep the extracted tar for a token you just captured in the proxy — **matching bytes is the proof**.
items.escalation: -> D11 (what is stored) -> D13 (replay the token). Twin rows: D03-068 and D11-051 — mark them from `logs/D02-031.txt`; do not re-run. Note the framing that does **not** pay: H1 #1225158 (Zivver), "ADB Backup is enabled within AndroidManifest", awarded **$0** — the manifest flag alone was the entire report.
items.ruled_out_when: `adb backup` produces a `.ab` of trivial size (header only) or fails outright, **and** `targetSdk >= 31` with `debuggable` absent, **and** `dataExtractionRules` excludes the sensitive paths. Verify empirically — `adb backup` support varies by OEM and OS version; do not assume from the manifest in either direction.

items.title: `setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true)` shipped unconditionally
items.vrt: `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (P1) when the WebView session cookie/JWT read from DevTools replays successfully
items.attacker: AM-11 physical unlocked with USB debugging; AM-03 for a local app on the same device that can reach the abstract socket
items.applies_to: All. This flag is **independent** of `android:debuggable` — an app can be non-debuggable and still expose DevTools. The call must be guarded by `ApplicationInfo.FLAG_DEBUGGABLE` to pass.
items.maps_to: MASTG-TEST-0227 (Debugging Enabled for WebViews), MASWE-0063, MASTG-KNOW-0028, MASTG-TECH-0142
items.test: If called unconditionally, a connected host attaches Chrome DevTools to **every** WebView in the app, reads the DOM and `localStorage`, and executes JS in the page's origin.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rn 'setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled' $DEC/jadx/sources/
grep -rn -B3 -A3 'setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled' $DEC/jadx/sources/ | grep -n 'FLAG_DEBUGGABLE\|BuildConfig.DEBUG'
adb shell cat /proc/net/unix | grep -i webview_devtools_remote
# then open chrome://inspect/#devices on the host
```
items.proof: A `@webview_devtools_remote_<pid>` abstract socket for the target PID in `/proc/net/unix`, and the app's WebView appearing under `chrome://inspect/#devices`. Then read `document.cookie` / `localStorage` from the DevTools console and replay the value against the API.
items.escalation: -> D15 session replay; -> D10 (the DevTools console lets you call any `@JavascriptInterface` bridge method directly, turning a bridge audit into a live one).
items.ruled_out_when: The call site is absent, **or** it is guarded by `(getApplicationInfo().flags & ApplicationInfo.FLAG_DEBUGGABLE) != 0` / `BuildConfig.DEBUG` **and** `/proc/net/unix` shows no `webview_devtools_remote` socket for the app's PID on a release build. Grep-only negatives are insufficient — check the socket at runtime, because a bundled SDK can enable it (-> D02-034).

items.title: `android:testOnly="true"` — you were handed the wrong binary
items.severity_note: Low (but it invalidates the engagement scope; raise it immediately)
items.vrt: — (scope control)
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: developer.android.com/guide/topics/manifest/application-element
items.test: `android:testOnly` marks the app installable only via `adb` and unpublishable to Play. Its presence in a build handed to you as "production" means you are not testing the shipping artefact — every finding you write is about a binary no user has.
items.how:
```bash
aapt2 dump xmltree base.apk --file AndroidManifest.xml | grep -iE 'testOnly|allowClearUserData|debuggable'
```
items.proof: `android:testOnly(0x01010272)=(type 0x12)0xffffffff` in the xmltree dump.
items.escalation: Stop and request the real release artefact. Then re-run D02-001 and D02-002 on it. A `testOnly` build is also typically debuggable, which is why testers mistake it for a D02-029 finding. Twin row: D03-071 — mark it from `logs/D02-033.txt`; do not re-run.
items.ruled_out_when: `testOnly` is absent from the xmltree dump **and** the artefact's signer matches the store artefact (D02-006). `android:allowClearUserData` (default `true`) is documented as applying to system apps — do not report its presence on a normal app.

items.title: `BuildConfig.DEBUG == true` inside a bundled AAR/JAR
items.severity_note: Medium — High when the debug branch disables TLS validation, enables a test backend, or logs credentials
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_internal_asset` (P3) when it exposes a staging backend; `mobile_security_misconfiguration.ssl_certificate_pinning.absent` (P5) when it only relaxes pinning
items.attacker: AM-06 network attacker (if the branch relaxes TLS) / AM-03 (if it enables verbose credential logging)
items.applies_to: All. The app module can be a correct release build while a bundled AAR/JAR was compiled with `DEBUG true`.
items.maps_to: MobSF rule `android_aar_jar_debug_enabled` (severity high, cvss 5.4, masvs `resilience-2`), pattern `class BuildConfig` AND `DEBUG.*?true`
items.test: Find every `BuildConfig` class in the decompiled tree — not just the app's — and then find what the flag actually gates.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rn --include='*.java' -E 'class BuildConfig' "$DEC/jadx/sources"
grep -rn --include='*.java' -E 'DEBUG *= *true' "$DEC/jadx/sources"
grep -rn --include='*.java' -E 'BuildConfig\.DEBUG' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | head -50
```
items.proof: A decompiled `BuildConfig` with `public static final boolean DEBUG = true` in a package that is **not** the app's own, plus a reachable branch guarded by it that changes security behaviour (e.g. `if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) trustAllCerts()`), plus the behaviour observed at runtime.
items.escalation: -> D14 (pinning or validation bypass baked into the shipped build — and note the SDK did this, the developer did not) -> D20 (credential logging) -> D18 (the SDK responsible).
items.ruled_out_when: Every `BuildConfig.DEBUG` in the tree is `false`, **or** the `true` ones gate only logging that you confirmed produces no sensitive output at runtime (`adb logcat` while driving the auth flow), **or** R8 has already stripped the guarded branch — verify with `dexdump`/jadx that the branch body survived, not just that the constant exists.

items.title: Debug/QA components and hidden menus surviving into the release variant
items.severity_note: High when the feature bypasses authentication, entitlement or payment; Medium when it only discloses configuration
items.vrt: `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (P1) for an auth-bypass menu; `broken_access_control.exposed_sensitive_android_intent` (varies — rated on what it exposes) for the component itself
items.applies_to: All. `targetSdk < 31`: components with an `<intent-filter>` default to exported. `android:exported="false"` is explicitly **insufficient** protection for a debug component — documented guidance is that on a rooted device, or when debuggable is enabled, ADB can still reach it.
items.maps_to: developer.android.com risk article `test-debug` (MASVS-CODE: Code Quality); MASWE-0063, MASWE-0061 (Debug Artifacts Not Removed)
items.test: Hunt build-variant leakage: staging endpoints, auth-bypass toggles, payment-skip switches, "developer options" activities — and the library debug components whose names contain no 'debug' at all.
items.how:
```bash
grep -niE 'debug|test|qa|staging|internal|dev|mock|sandbox|bypass' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rn 'BuildConfig\.\(DEBUG\|FLAVOR\|BUILD_TYPE\)' $DEC/jadx/sources/
grep -rniE '(skipAuth|bypassLogin|forceEntitled|isTestUser|mockPayment|debugMenu|enableStaging)' $DEC/jadx/sources/
adb shell am start -n com.target.app/.DebugSettingsActivity
adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep topResumedActivity
# library debug components that leak into release builds (the names do not contain 'debug'):
grep -nE 'androidx\.compose\.ui\.tooling\.PreviewActivity|leakcanary|\.stetho\.|DebugActivity|TestActivity|flipper' "$DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml"
# PreviewActivity invokes any @Composable named in its `composable` extra; recent ui-tooling versions guard it with a runtime
# FLAG_DEBUGGABLE check, older ones do not — read the guard, do not assume it
grep -rn -A8 'class PreviewActivity' "$DEC/jadx/sources/androidx/compose/ui/tooling/" | grep -nE 'FLAG_DEBUGGABLE|isDebuggable|ApplicationInfo'
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell am start -n "$PKG/androidx.compose.ui.tooling.PreviewActivity" --es composable '<fqcn>Kt.<PreviewFn>'
```
items.proof: The debug activity renders (screenshot with `topResumedActivity` confirming it is yours); an exported `PreviewActivity` with no `FLAG_DEBUGGABLE` guard (or on a debuggable build, D02-029) rendering a composable you named from an unprivileged app; or a `BuildConfig.DEBUG`-guarded branch is reachable because the release build still contains the staging base URL — prove it by pointing the app at that host through the proxy and getting a 200 from staging.
items.escalation: Auth-bypass menus chain directly into D15 (account takeover) and D23 (entitlement fraud). A staging host reached from a release build is a D15 shadow-API entry point with weaker controls.
items.ruled_out_when: `am start` against every candidate component returns `SecurityException: Permission Denial: ... not exported` from a non-root shell, **and** the staging base URL is absent from the release strings/assets, **and** each `BuildConfig.DEBUG` branch body was stripped by R8. Bundle this with `android:debuggable` (D02-029), `setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled` (D02-032) and native debug symbols (D16) into **one** "debug artefacts shipped to production" item rather than four Lows.

items.title: Debug-only deep links and debug navigation routes in the release manifest
items.severity_note: Medium (High if the route exposes data or state rather than only crashing)
items.vrt: `application_level_denial_of_service_dos.app_crash.malformed_android_intents` (**P5**) for a crash-only route; `broken_access_control.exposed_sensitive_android_intent` (varies) when it exposes data
items.attacker: AM-03 zero-permission local app (any installed app can fire the intent); AM-02 if the scheme is web-reachable
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: MASWE-0061 (Debug Artifacts Not Removed); H1 #3829030 (Yelp Business, Low 3.3 — `yelp-biz:///debug_navigation` crashed the app *and* invalidated the session); H1 #3399016 (Nextcloud, None 0.0 — crash-only DoS scored zero)
items.test: Debug routes left reachable from an exported filter. The severity hinges entirely on whether the session survives the crash — a pure crash scores near zero.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rniE 'debug|staging|internal|qa[_-]|dev[_-]|test[_-]' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml | grep -iE 'scheme|host|path|name='
adb logcat -c && adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "<scheme>:///<debugroute>" \
  && adb logcat -d | grep -iE 'FATAL|AndroidRuntime'
# then reopen the app and check whether you are still signed in
```
items.proof: `adb logcat` showing a fatal exception, and reopening the app presenting the login screen. Yelp's report evidenced the persistent-logout loop by re-running `am start` in a `while true` shell loop.
items.escalation: -> D09 (the deep-link surface itself) -> D13 if the crash drops session state.
items.ruled_out_when: No debug-named scheme/host/path appears in the merged manifest, **or** firing every candidate route produces no fatal exception **and** the session survives (check by making an authenticated API call from the app after the attempt). Always test the session effect — the difference between Low 3.3 and None 0.0 in the corpus is exactly that.

items.title: Build residue shipped inside the package: mapping files, unstripped symbols, source maps
items.severity_note: Medium — High when a shipped source map or mapping file exposes the encryption routine you then reimplement
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.sensitive_data_hardcoded.file_paths` (P5) for paths alone; the real routing follows whatever the residue lets you recover
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: hackwithsingh sec-14-5 #6, sec-14-18 #10; MASTG-TECH-0007 (Exploring the App Package); MASTG-TEST-0288 (Debugging Symbols in Native Binaries), MASWE-0061 (Debug Artifacts Not Removed), MASTG-KNOW-0008
items.test: Look inside the APK/AAB for shipped build residue that hands you the source model — ProGuard mapping, unstripped `.so` symbols, JS source maps, `BuildConfig` debug constants, `.properties` version markers.
items.how:
```bash
unzip -l base.apk | grep -Ei 'mapping|\.map$|\.properties$|\.json$|source|BUNDLE-METADATA'
# the two AGP-generated metadata files every 2024+ release carries — neither matches the patterns above
unzip -p apk/base.apk META-INF/version-control-info.textproto 2>/dev/null   # AGP 8.3+ default (android.vcsInfo.include): repository system, local_root_path, revision <git sha>
unzip -p apk/base.apk META-INF/com/android/build/gradle/app-metadata.properties 2>/dev/null   # androidGradlePluginVersion -> toolchain date
unzip -Z1 apk/base.apk | grep -E 'META-INF/(version-control-info|.*\.kotlin_module|.*\.version$)|assets/dexopt/baseline\.prof'
for so in $(find "$DEC/apktool/lib" -name '*.so'); do file "$so"; llvm-nm -D "$so" 2>/dev/null | head -3; done   # llvm-nm: macOS has no GNU nm
grep -rn 'BuildConfig' "$DEC"/apktool/smali*/ | head
grep -rn 'DEBUG = true\|STAGING\|API_KEY' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | head
```
items.proof: `file` reporting "not stripped" on a shipped `.so`, a `.map` file in `assets/`, or a `mapping.txt` inside the package. `revision: "<40-hex>"` in `version-control-info.textproto` pins the shipped build to a commit — record it in D02-001's manifest and D02-008's correspondence note; alone it is `sensitive_data_hardcoded.file_paths` (P5), reportable only through what the commit unlocks (a leaked or public repository, D02-062).
items.escalation: Symbols -> D16 native analysis; a source map -> D19 (the un-minified JS bundle); a shipped mapping file also satisfies D02-007 for free.
items.ruled_out_when: No `.map`/`mapping.txt` in the archive, every `lib/*.so` reports "stripped", `.properties` files carry no version or endpoint data, and `version-control-info.textproto` is absent (or the build set `vcsInfo.include=false`). Note that `BUNDLE-METADATA/` inside an `.aab` is **not** packaged into APKs — finding a mapping there is expected and is not a finding against the shipped app.

items.title: Base-only install: does the app fail closed without its required splits
items.severity_note: High when the missing split is the one performing attestation, licensing or integrity checking
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies) when the removed module was the control; `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (P1) if the removed module performed the auth gate
items.applies_to: Apps shipped as AAB with dynamic feature modules or config splits (`android:isSplitRequired`)
items.maps_to: developer.android.com/guide/app-bundle/play-feature-delivery ("Apps must verify module installation before accessing code/resources via `SplitInstallManager.getInstalledModules()`")
items.test: Bundled apps normally refuse to run without their required splits. Check whether the app degrades **open** rather than failing closed when a split is absent — you have then removed a control by omission, without touching the signature of `base.apk`.
items.how:
```bash
grep -i 'isSplitRequired' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
adb -s "$SERIAL" uninstall "$PKG"
adb -s "$SERIAL" install --no-incremental base.apk            # base only, no splits
adb logcat -c; adb shell monkey -p com.target.app 1; adb logcat -d | grep -iE 'split|SplitCompat|missing'
# compare with the full set:
adb -s "$SERIAL" install-multiple --no-incremental -r base.apk split_config.*.apk
```
items.proof: The app launches base-only and a feature guarded by `SplitInstallManager.getInstalledModules()` is reachable anyway (the module check returns false but the code path proceeds), or the integrity/licensing module is simply absent and its checks never run. Screenshot both the base-only launch and the reached feature.
items.escalation: -> D21 (RASP/attestation removal with `base.apk`'s signature intact — a far cleaner story than patching smali) -> D23 if the removed module held licensing.
items.ruled_out_when: `adb install base.apk` fails with a missing-split error, **or** the app launches and immediately terminates with a documented missing-module message, **or** every module-gated code path is preceded by a `getInstalledModules()` check that actually blocks (prove by reaching the code path, not by reading the source). A crash on missing split is **correct** behaviour — do not file it as a DoS (`application_level_denial_of_service_dos.app_crash` is P5).

items.title: `SplitInstallManager.getInstalledModules()` not checked before using module code
items.severity_note: Support (it is the mechanism behind D02-038) — Medium when it produces a reachable uninitialised state
items.vrt: — (mechanism; the finding is rated under D02-038)
items.applies_to: Play Feature Delivery apps (on-demand, conditional and instant modules)
items.maps_to: developer.android.com/guide/app-bundle/play-feature-delivery
items.test: Find every entry point into a dynamic feature module and check whether the installation state is verified first. Dynamic feature modules are also delivered *at runtime*, which makes them a dynamic-code-loading surface in their own right.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'SplitInstallManager|SplitInstallRequest|getInstalledModules|SplitCompat\.install|SplitInstallHelper' $DEC/jadx/sources/
grep -rn 'dist:module\|dist:onDemand\|dist:instant' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml "$E"/work/aab/base/manifest/* 2>/dev/null   # the second path is the unzipped .aab (D02-005)
```
Then drive each entry point with the module absent (per D02-038) and observe.
items.proof: A call into module code with no preceding `getInstalledModules().contains(...)` guard, and the resulting behaviour on a base-only install.
items.escalation: -> D02-038 for the severity; -> D17 because the module itself is code delivered after install and its delivery channel is in scope.
items.ruled_out_when: Every module entry point is guarded, and the guard blocks (verified by reaching it on a base-only install), **or** the app has no dynamic feature modules — `grep 'dist:module'` empty and `isSplitRequired` absent.

items.title: Code and native libraries that exist only in a config split
items.severity_note: High (the severity of whatever the split-only code leaks or exposes)
items.vrt: Follows the content — commonly `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.*` or `broken_access_control.exposed_sensitive_android_intent` (varies)
items.attacker: n/a (inventory step) — the finding it uncovers inherits its own attacker model
items.applies_to: All AAB/XAPK/split-delivery apps; universally true for Flutter (`libapp.so`), React Native and Unity (`libil2cpp.so`) builds
items.maps_to: MASTG-TECH-0145 (Working with XAPK Files), MASTG-TECH-0003
items.test: `config.arm64_v8a` and `config.<lang>` splits sometimes carry different code paths, different strings, and the native libraries the base APK does not contain. Testing only `base.apk` produces false "not present" conclusions and a silently incomplete assessment.
items.how:
```bash
ls -d "$DEC"/apktool/*/ "$DEC"/jadx/sources >/dev/null    # every split is decompiled in P2: per-split apktool trees at $DEC/apktool/<split-basename>/, one jadx tree over base + splits
unzip -l splits/split_config.arm64_v8a.apk | grep -E 'libapp|libflutter|libil2cpp|libassemblies|\.so$'
for f in splits/*.apk; do echo "== $f"; aapt2 d xmltree "$f" --file AndroidManifest.xml \
  | grep -E 'E: (activity|service|receiver|provider|uses-permission)'; done
```
Fast fallback when jadx is slow or fails on obfuscated DEX:
```bash
find splits -name 'classes*.dex' -exec strings -8 {} \; > strings_all.txt
```
items.proof: A component, permission, native library or hardcoded string present in a split and absent from `base.apk`, with its own exported/permission attributes quoted from the split's own manifest.
items.escalation: Split-only `.so` -> D16; split-only component -> D03/D04/D06/D07; split-only string -> D18.
items.ruled_out_when: Every split's manifest declares no components or permissions beyond the base's, every split's DEX (if any) contains only resource stubs, and `unzip -l` on each split shows no `.so`. Confirm you have the *complete* split set first (D02-004) — this item cannot be ruled out on an incomplete set.

items.title: Re-signing and reinstalling a split set correctly
items.applies_to: All split/AAB-delivered apps
items.maps_to: MASTG-TOOL-0103 (uber-apk-signer); HN Security multi-APK `pm install-create` / `install-write` / `install-commit` flow
items.test: A repack of `base.apk` alone will not install over a split-delivered app. Every split must be rebuilt and re-signed with the **same** key and installed in one session.
items.how:
```bash
for f in splits/*.apk; do
  zipalign -P 16 -f 4 "$f" "aligned_$(basename "$f")"
  apksigner sign --ks key.jks --ks-pass pass:android --v4-signing-enabled false "aligned_$(basename "$f")"   # no .idsig beside the output
done
adb -s "$SERIAL" install-multiple --no-incremental -r aligned_base.apk aligned_split_config.*.apk   # .idsig files beside the APKs otherwise force incremental mode: 'Incremental installation not allowed' hides the verdict
# session form, when install-multiple is unavailable:
adb shell pm install-create -r
adb shell pm install-write -S <size> <session> 0 /data/local/tmp/base.apk
adb shell pm install-commit <session>
```
items.proof: The reinstalled modified split set launches, and `adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep topResumedActivity` shows the screen under test reached — a silently broken rebuild is indistinguishable from a fixed bug.
items.escalation: Enables D02-022 on bundled apps; mandatory before D02-038's comparison arm.
items.ruled_out_when: n/a — this is the procedure. If it fails, the cause is either mixed signing keys across splits or a `.locals` verifier crash (D02-023), not an app-side integrity control; distinguish before you claim one.

items.title: `lib-*/` and extracted-native-library drop zones
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies) — realistically rated as arbitrary code execution in the app UID; `insecure_data_transport.executable_download.no_secure_integrity_check` (P4) if the library arrives over a channel
items.attacker: AM-03 zero-permission local app with any file-write primitive into the app's data dir
items.applies_to: All. The Android 10 (targetSdk 29) W^X change removes `exec()` of files in the app home directory (SELinux `execute_no_trans` on `app_data_file`); it does **not** stop `System.load()`/`dlopen()` of a `.so` from a writable app path, nor `DexClassLoader` on a writable DEX — the `lib-*/`/extraction drop zone is unaffected. Android 14 (targetSdk 34) requires files handed to a class loader (DEX/JAR/APK) to be read-only or the loader throws; it does not cover `.so` loaded via `System.load`.
items.maps_to: H1 #1377748 (Evernote, High), #1115864 (Mattermost, High 7.8), #1362313 (Evernote, sibling report); ATT&CK T1407; developer.android.com "Dynamic code loading" storage guidance
items.test: `/data/data/<pkg>/lib-*/` is loaded at process start. Any primitive that writes an attacker-chosen filename into the app's data directory becomes persistent arbitrary code execution. Separately, some apps extract `.so`/`.dex`/`.apk` payloads out of `assets/` at runtime — each extraction step is an attacker-writable code path, and the **file mode** decides the severity. Also `<dataDir>/cache/oat_primary/<isa>/base.art` — an ART runtime app image generated into the app's own cache (Android 14+) and mapped at startup. Evaluate, do not assume: ART validates image headers and checksums against the APK's oat/vdex; a substituted image that fails validation is discarded (a Support note for D07), one that is accepted is persistent execution in the app's UID.
items.how:
```bash
unzip -l base.apk | grep -E 'assets/.*\.(so|apk|jar|dex|zip|bin)$'
grep -i 'extractNativeLibs' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
adb shell run-as com.target.app ls -la /data/data/com.target.app/      # lib-1, lib-main, files, cache
adb shell 'ls -lRZ /data/data/com.target.app/ | grep -E "\.so|\.apk|\.jar|\.dex"'
frida-trace -D "$SERIAL" -n "$PKG" -j 'java.util.zip.ZipInputStream!getNextEntry' -j 'java.io.FileOutputStream!$init'
# Android 14+ ART writes a runtime app image into the APP-WRITABLE cache and maps it on the next start
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell "run-as $PKG ls -l cache/oat_primary/*/"                      # base.art (sometimes base.odex/.vdex), owned by the app, rw
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell "run-as $PKG sh -c 'grep -E \"oat_primary|base\\.art\" /proc/\$(pidof -s $PKG)/maps'"
# after triggering a write primitive, confirm the drop landed:
adb shell run-as com.target.app ls -la /data/data/com.target.app/lib-1/
```
items.proof: Your `.so`, built for the device's actual ABI, sitting in `lib-1/` (or `lib-main/`) under the name of a library the app loads (`libjnigraphics.so`, `libyoga.so`), plus a callback on next app launch — Evernote #1377748 proved it with `nc 127.0.0.1 6666` from an adb shell after restart. For the extraction variant, a `.so`/`.dex` written into `files/` or `code_cache/` whose mode from `ls -lZ` is anything other than `-r--------`.
items.escalation: -> D16 (the native surface you just entered) -> D17 (the loader) -> D07 (a FileProvider path traversal is the usual delivery of the write primitive) -> D11.
items.ruled_out_when: No file-write primitive reaches the app's data directory from a zero-permission app (test it, do not assume), **and** every native load reads only from `nativeLibraryDir` (`/data/app/.../lib/<abi>`, not app-writable) — no `System.load(<path under /data/data or /data/user>)`, no SoLoader/ReLinker-style extraction directory — **and**, for the DEX variant, `targetSdk >= 34` with the loaded file set read-only before load (`ls -lZ` shows `-r--------`). `targetSdk >= 29` rules out nothing here: it blocks `exec()`, not loaders. A writable drop zone with no reachable write primitive is a Support observation for D07, not a finding here.

items.title: Merged-manifest diff: components and permissions no first-party code declared
items.severity_note: Medium standalone; High when a library-contributed provider is exported and leaks app data
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.exposed_sensitive_android_intent` (varies — rated on what it exposes)
items.applies_to: All. `targetSdk < 17`: providers exported by default. `targetSdk < 31`: components with an `<intent-filter>` exported by default.
items.maps_to: MASTG-TECH-0141 (Inspecting the Merged AndroidManifest), MASTG-TOOL-0007 (Android Studio), MASTG-KNOW-0004
items.test: Third-party AARs contribute `<activity>`, `<provider>`, `<receiver>` and `<uses-permission>` entries into the merged manifest. They are part of the shipped attack surface and are routinely missed because they are not in `app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`.
items.how:
With source, Android Studio's **Merged Manifest** tab attributes each element to its contributing library. CLI:
```bash
./gradlew app:processReleaseManifest
cat app/build/intermediates/merged_manifests/release/AndroidManifest.xml
```
Black-box, the shipped APK's manifest **is** the merged manifest — attribute each element by namespace:
```bash
apkanalyzer manifest print base.apk > merged.xml
grep -oE 'android:name="[^"]+"' merged.xml | sort -u | grep -viE '"com\.target\.'
aapt2 dump permissions base.apk
```
items.proof: A `<provider>` or `<receiver>` in the shipped manifest that maps to a library package (e.g. a `FileProvider` with a library authority), plus a `<uses-permission>` no first-party code uses. Name the contributing library.
items.escalation: -> D07 (library FileProviders with a `<root-path>`) -> D18 (SDK-declared components) -> D05 (library receivers) -> D20 (undisclosed collection under an SDK-added permission, which is also a Play data-safety mismatch).
items.ruled_out_when: Every component and permission in the merged manifest maps to a first-party namespace or an SDK you have accounted for and tested, and each SDK-contributed component is `exported="false"` with no `<intent-filter>` — verified by `am start` / `drozer` attempts from an unprivileged context, not by reading the attribute.

items.title: Manifest-merger creep: an SDK re-opened cleartext or replaced the network security config
items.severity_note: High when the merged value is `usesCleartextTraffic="true"` or a permissive `networkSecurityConfig` that re-opens a network finding you would otherwise concede as mitigated (permission over-grant is D02-043's test)
items.vrt: Routes to the network finding it re-enables
items.attacker: AM-06 network attacker (cleartext), AM-08 (the SDK that did it)
items.applies_to: All Gradle-built apps. The merger report exists only with source access — the black-box fallback is below. `targetSdk < 28`: cleartext is allowed by default anyway, so the merged value only matters at 28+.
items.maps_to: Android manifest-merger report at `app/build/outputs/logs/manifest-merger-<variant>-report.txt`
items.test: A dependency can add a dangerous permission, re-enable `usesCleartextTraffic`, or replace the `networkSecurityConfig` reference through ordinary merger rules — and neither the developer nor a source-only reviewer will see it. Nobody diffs the developer's source manifest against the merged manifest.
items.how:
With source:
```bash
cat app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -nE 'ADDED from|MERGED from|IMPLIED|usesCleartextTraffic|uses-permission|provider|receiver|networkSecurityConfig' \
  app/build/outputs/logs/manifest-merger-release-report.txt
```
Without source (permission over-grant is enumerated once in D02-043 — do not repeat `aapt2 dump permissions` here):
```bash
grep -nE 'usesCleartextTraffic|networkSecurityConfig' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
cat $DEC/apktool/res/xml/network_security_config.xml 2>/dev/null
grep -rnE 'android:name="(com|io|net|org)\.' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml | grep -viE 'com\.target\.'
```
items.proof: A merger-report line reading `ADDED from [com.vendor:sdk:x.y.z] AndroidManifest.xml:NN` next to a dangerous permission or `android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"`, alongside the developer's own manifest that does not contain it. Black-box: the attribute present in the shipped manifest with no first-party justification, plus the SDK namespace that owns it.
items.escalation: -> D14 (cleartext re-enabled, or an `overridePins="true"` anchor you did not expect) -> D18 (the SDK) -> D20 (undisclosed data collection under the added permission).
items.ruled_out_when: The merger report shows no `ADDED from` line for any security-relevant attribute, **or** black-box, `usesCleartextTraffic` is absent/false, the NSC is first-party, and every permission maps to first-party code. Note that `overridePins="true"` outside a debug-only `<debug-overrides>` block is a finding in its own right (-> D14).

items.title: Resource-level feature gating flipped and rebuilt
items.severity_note: High when the unlocked function performs a privileged **server-side** action; Low if the server independently rejects it
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies) / `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (P1) if it exposes an admin registration flow that the server honours
items.attacker: AM-03 (an attacker running a repacked client against their own account) / AM-05 another user of the same app
items.applies_to: All; depends on the absence of an integrity check (D02-022) and a decorative integrity signal (D02-021)
items.maps_to: sec-88 "Hacking InsecureBankv2 App" — Privilege Escalation section (`res/values/strings.xml`, `is_admin` = no -> yes)
items.test: Search resources for booleans and strings that **gate functionality** rather than merely style it. If the server does not re-check the role, flipping the resource unlocks the feature.
items.how:
```bash
cp -r "$DEC/apktool" "$E/work/D02-045/"     # work on a copy; the canonical P2 tree stays pristine
grep -rniE '(is_admin|is_premium|isDebug|enable_[a-z_]+|feature_flag|show_[a-z_]+)' "$E/work/D02-045/res/values/"
# in jadx, locate getString(R.string.is_admin) / getBoolean(R.bool.*) in the gating Activity
perl -pi -e 's|<string name="is_admin">no</string>|<string name="is_admin">yes</string>|' "$E/work/D02-045/res/values/strings.xml"   # perl -pi is identical on GNU and BSD; sed in-place editing has no portable form
grep -c 'is_admin">yes' "$E/work/D02-045/res/values/strings.xml"     # must print 1 before apktool b
apktool b "$E/work/D02-045" -o patched.apk
zipalign -P 16 -f 4 patched.apk aligned.apk
apksigner sign --ks key.jks --ks-pass pass:android --v4-signing-enabled false aligned.apk
adb -s "$SERIAL" install --no-incremental -r aligned.apk      # an .idsig beside the APK otherwise forces incremental mode and hides the install verdict
```

items.how:
```bash
# raw unzip trees from D01-022 live under $E/work/raw/<split-basename>/ (one archive per unzip call)
find "$E"/work/raw -type f \( -name '*.jks' -o -name '*.keystore' -o -name '*.bks' -o -name '*.p12' -o -name '*.pfx' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name '*.key' \) -print
grep -ral -- '-----BEGIN \(RSA \|EC \|DSA \|\)PRIVATE KEY-----' "$E"/work/raw/
grep -ral 'PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK' "$E"/work/raw/
# BKS is a BouncyCastle format: stock keytool answers "BKS not found" without the provider jar
keytool -list -v -keystore "$DEC/apktool/res/raw/foo.bks" -storetype BKS -storepass '' \
  -providerclass org.bouncycastle.jce.provider.BouncyCastleProvider -providerpath "$BCPROV" 2>&1 | head   # BCPROV=/path/to/bcprov-jdk18on-<ver>.jar
keytool -list -v -keystore "$DEC/apktool/assets/client.p12" -storetype PKCS12 -storepass '' 2>&1 | head   # PKCS12/JKS need no provider
openssl pkey -in "$E/work/raw/base/assets/client.pem" -noout -text | head
apkleaks -f base.apk
```
items.proof: `keytool -list` enumerating a `PrivateKeyEntry`, or `openssl` parsing the PEM — i.e. you hold the private half of a key the app uses for signing, mTLS or pinning. Then perform **one** authenticated request with it and stop: HackerOne Platform Standards state that hackers "should NOT test their validity beyond authenticating and then immediately deauthenticating".
items.escalation: -> D15 (impersonate the app to the API, defeating client attestation) -> D14 (forge a pinned chain if the bundled key is a CA) -> D12 (if it is a content-signing key, forge receipts and licence responses).

A password-protected keystore is **not** ruled out until you have tried the empty password, `android`, and any password string found in the package. `BKS not found` is a tooling error (missing BouncyCastle provider), not an empty keystore.

items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: MASTG-TEST-0212 (hardcoded symmetric keys), MASWE-0004 (CWE-312, 321, 540, 798), MASVS-STORAGE-1, Mobile Top 10 2024 M1; MASTG-TOOL-0144 (gitleaks), MASTG-TOOL-0125 (apkleaks); HackerOne Platform Standards "Bounty Awards for Discovered Leaked Credentials"
items.record: `logs/D02-047.txt` (every probe's raw response), `logs/D02-047-grep.txt` (the regex sweep with the control line count), `logs/D02-047-gitleaks.json`
items.test: Extract every credential-looking string from the artefact, then **prove liveness** against the real service. A hardcoded string with no proven access is a P5. This is the single item in D02 that reliably reaches P1.
items.how:
```bash
# sweep EVERY split (split-only strings exist: D02-040); the decompiled trees already live in $DEC (base at $DEC/apktool, per-split trees at $DEC/apktool/<split-basename>/)
ls "$DEC"/apktool/*/AndroidManifest.xml | wc -l          # must equal the split count from D02-004
# 1. the regex sweep is PRIMARY; gitleaks and apkleaks are secondary (both have false-negatived on res/values/strings.xml in practice)
grep -rEn '(AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|sk_live_[0-9a-zA-Z]{24,}|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----|xox[baprs]-|ghp_[0-9A-Za-z]{36}|SG\.[0-9A-Za-z_-]{22}\.[0-9A-Za-z_-]{43})' "$DEC/apktool" | tee logs/D02-047-grep.txt | wc -l
# 2. positive control — plant one synthetic key and prove the sweep sees it; a sweep that misses the control is broken, the app is not clean
mkdir -p "$DEC/apktool/res/raw"; printf 'AIzaSyA%032d\n' 0 > "$DEC/apktool/res/raw/_d02047_control.txt"; grep -rEl 'AIzaSyA0{32}' "$DEC/apktool" | grep -c _d02047_control; rm "$DEC/apktool/res/raw/_d02047_control.txt"
# 3. gitleaks >= 8.19: `dir` takes ONE path (several paths silently scan 0 bytes); `detect --no-git` is the deprecated spelling
gitleaks dir "$DEC/apktool" --report-path logs/D02-047-gitleaks.json -v; grep -c '"RuleID"' logs/D02-047-gitleaks.json
# 4. apkleaks re-runs jadx internally (15–20 min on a large base): run it once per split in the background and pre-filter the
#    JSON_Web_Token bucket (bundled public-suffix lists) and Facebook_Secret_Key bucket (any 32-hex string) before reading it (D01-064 has the jq filter)
for a in apk/*.apk; do apkleaks -f "$a" --json -o "logs/D02-047-apkleaks-$(basename "$a" .apk).json" & done; wait
unzip -p apk/base.apk 'lib/*/*.so' 'assets/*' 'res/raw/*' 2>/dev/null | strings -n 12 | grep -Ei 'secret|token|api[_-]?key|password|bearer' | sort -u
grep -rEn 'new SecretKeySpec\(|SecretKeySpec\(.*getBytes' "$DEC/jadx/sources"
grep -rEn 'https?://[a-z0-9.\-]+' "$DEC"/apktool/*/res/values/strings.xml | sort -u
```
Then exercise it, once — and record the raw response in `logs/D02-047.txt`; if the engagement already holds a restriction probe for the same key (D01-064, D18-009, D26-024), reuse it: every probe creates state on the vendor's project. For a Google `AIza` key use the full 39-character value (`AIza` + 35): a truncated key answers `API_KEY_INVALID` and reads as dead when it is live. Decode the probe: HTTP 200 = live, unrestricted; 403 with `API_KEY_ANDROID_APP_BLOCKED` / `API_KEY_HTTP_REFERRER_BLOCKED` = live, restricted to an app or referrer identity; 400 `API_KEY_INVALID` = dead. An Android-app restriction is not a security boundary — it is enforced from request headers any client can set; re-send once with `-H "X-Android-Package: $PKG" -H "X-Android-Cert: <signer SHA-1, hex, no colons>"` (both values are public: the package name and the D02-011 digest). A 200 on that retry means the restriction is decorative; rate by what the enabled APIs return — billing-only data = `pay_per_use_abuse` (P4), user/tenant data = `for_publicly_accessible_asset` (P1). `aws sts get-caller-identity`; the relevant Google API endpoint for an `AIza` key; `auth.test` for a Slack token. **Stop immediately after proving identity — do not enumerate data.**
items.proof: The HTTP 200 (or the `GetCallerIdentity` ARN) returned by the third party using the extracted key, side by side with the file and line where it was found, and the artefact hash from D02-001. For a cross-tenant case, a request from your own laptop, authenticating only with the extracted credential, returning data belonging to another tenant.
items.escalation: -> D18 (a live cloud key is the entry point to the whole cloud surface) -> D12 (a hardcoded *crypto* key decrypts the app's local ciphertext) -> D11 (the plaintext token behind it) -> D15.
items.ruled_out_when: Every candidate string is provably a public-by-design value (a Firebase web API key), **or** authentication with it fails from a clean host with the full-length key, **or** the key is restricted *and* every API enabled on it returns only public or billable data (checked with the header retry above — a package+SHA-1 restriction alone is never the boundary). The regex sweep showed the planted control, or nothing was ruled out. Twin rows: D01-064 and D11-027 — mark them from `logs/D02-047.txt`; do not re-run. Two routing traps: a Firebase/Maps key is `intentionally_public_sample_or_invalid` (P5) or `pay_per_use_abuse` (P4), not P1; and an **OAuth `client_secret` found in a mobile app is `sensitive_data_exposure.sensitive_data_hardcoded.oauth_secret` (P5) and sits on the never-submit list** — a public client is not supposed to hold a confidential secret, so the reportable finding is **PKCE non-enforcement** on the authorisation server (-> D13), not the secret's presence.

items.severity_note: Medium (the severity comes from what the hidden code does)

If the APK's code is compressed into a single opaque file or a packer is in use, a static-only report is incomplete. Run the app and collect the decompressed files, or dump DEX from memory. **Packing alone is informational** — escalate only when the unpacked stage does something the store listing and privacy policy do not describe.
items.how:
```bash
apkid base.apk                       # identify compiler / packer / obfuscator
# entropy sweep for an encrypted blob
for f in $(unzip -Z1 base.apk 'assets/*' 'lib/*' 'res/raw/*'); do
  unzip -p base.apk "$f" | ent 2>/dev/null | awk -v n="$f" '/Entropy/ {print n, $0}'
done
# maintained route first: memory-scan every mapped DEX header after the packer has decrypted it, then diff the class lists
pip install frida-dexdump && frida-dexdump -D "$SERIAL" -f "$PKG" -o dumps/
apkid dumps/*.dex && jadx -d "$E/work/D02-049/jadx-runtime" dumps/*.dex
diff <(cd "$DEC/jadx/sources" && find . -name '*.java' | sort -u) <(cd "$E/work/D02-049/jadx-runtime/sources" && find . -name '*.java' | sort -u) | grep '^>' | head
# clsdumper only where it is installed in the harness (record the version; availability is not guaranteed):
clsdumper "$PKG" --spawn
clsdumper "$PKG" --strategies fart_dump,oat_extract --extract-classes
```
`clsdumper` phase 0 also blocks anti-instrumentation: it hooks `sigaction`/`signal` to stop crash and anti-debug handler registration, serves a filtered `/proc/self/maps` via `memfd_create`, and neutralises `pthread_create` watchdogs.

items.ruled_out_when: `apkid` reports no packer, `classes*.dex` decompiles cleanly in jadx, and the runtime class list matches the static one. **Never report "the app is packed" or "the app is not obfuscated"** — `lack_of_binary_hardening.lack_of_obfuscation` is P5 and Grab, Spotify, Starbucks and Xiaomi all list it out of scope verbatim.

items.title: `android:appComponentFactory` plus `createPackageContext` as a code-execution sink
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies) — arbitrary code execution in the victim app's process and UID
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: developer.android.com risk article `create-package-context` (MASVS-CODE: Code Quality)
items.test: A malicious app that claims a package name a victim passes to `createPackageContext()` and exports `android:appComponentFactory` achieves arbitrary code execution inside the victim. Audit **both** sides: does the target declare an `appComponentFactory`, and does it ever call `createPackageContext`?
items.how:
```bash
grep -n 'appComponentFactory' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rn 'createPackageContext' $DEC/jadx/sources/
grep -rn 'CONTEXT_INCLUDE_CODE\|CONTEXT_IGNORE_SECURITY' $DEC/jadx/sources/
```
items.proof: A call site matching `createPackageContext(pkg, Context.CONTEXT_IGNORE_SECURITY | Context.CONTEXT_INCLUDE_CODE)` followed by `getClassLoader()`, where `pkg` is a package not present on a clean device. Install a stub with that package name and an exported `appComponentFactory`, then prove execution with a file write from inside the victim's UID — a marker file under the victim's `files/`, visible via `run-as`, named with an 8+ character random string you confirmed is absent from the baseline app.
items.escalation: From inside the victim's UID everything in D11/D12/D13 is readable. Note that this mitigation depends on a correct signer check (D02-019) — a `signatures[0]` comparison does not save it.
items.ruled_out_when: No `createPackageContext` call site exists, **or** every call site passes a package name that is a compile-time constant *and* is signature-verified with `hasSigningCertificate(..., CERT_INPUT_SHA256)` before the context is created, **or** the flags omit `CONTEXT_INCLUDE_CODE` (resources-only contexts do not load code). Name, do not re-derive, the standard negative: platform-vendor services SDKs load their dynamic modules with `createPackageContext("<vendor services package>", CONTEXT_INCLUDE_CODE | CONTEXT_IGNORE_SECURITY)` (flags = 3) followed by a `DelegateLastClassLoader` over that package's module directory; the package name is a compile-time constant that cannot be claimed where the vendor package is preinstalled, and the SDK verifies the vendor package's signing certificate against a pinned set before creating the context. Record it as ruled out with the verifier class named (`logs/D02-050.txt`); the item applies to call sites whose package name is attacker-influenced or whose verifier is absent or `signatures[0]`-weak (D02-019).

items.vrt: `cryptographic_weakness.insufficient_verification_of_data_authenticity.cryptographic_signature` (varies) — a security control that reports success while performing no check

for m in re.finditer(r'<artifact name="([^"]+)">(.*?)</artifact>', x, re.S):

items.test: Maven `groupId` ownership is proved by DNS control of the reversed domain. If that domain has lapsed, an attacker registers it, claims the `groupId`, and publishes a new higher version of the library. Oversecured measured **3,710 of 26,163** mavenCentral domains (14.18%) as vulnerable and **18.18%** of dependencies interceptable across repositories.
items.how:
```bash
./gradlew :app:dependencies --configuration releaseRuntimeClasspath > deps.txt
```
```python
# reverse each groupId into a domain and check registrability — Python, not a shell loop
import re, subprocess, sys
groups = set()
for line in open('deps.txt'):
    m = re.search(r'([a-z0-9][a-z0-9.]+):([A-Za-z0-9._-]+):', line)
    if m: groups.add(m.group(1))
print(f"groupIds: {len(groups)}", file=sys.stderr)
checked = 0
for g in sorted(groups):
    dom = '.'.join(reversed(g.split('.')[:2])) if g.count('.') >= 1 else g
    try:
        out = subprocess.run(['whois', dom], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=20).stdout
        if re.search(r'No match|NOT FOUND|Status:\s*free|No Data Found', out, re.I):
            print("UNREGISTERED:", dom, "<-", g)
    except Exception as e:
        print("ERROR:", dom, e, file=sys.stderr)
    checked += 1
print(f"checked {checked}/{len(groups)}", file=sys.stderr)   # counts must match
```
```bash
ls gradle/verification-metadata.xml 2>/dev/null || echo "NO dependency verification configured"
gpg --keyserver keyserver.ubuntu.com --recv-keys <KEYID> && gpg --verify artifact.jar.asc
```
items.proof: A `groupId` in the **release runtime classpath** whose reversed domain is unregistered, expired or for sale, combined with the absence of `gradle/verification-metadata.xml` or with that artefact carrying no PGP signature. Oversecured's own finding that the default configuration does not validate dependencies in any way — and that even Google's artifacts are unsigned — is what makes this exploitable rather than theoretical.
items.escalation: -> D17 (arbitrary code in-process) and from there everything the app can do; build-time RCE -> CI signing-key access -> a malicious release signed with the client's real key.
items.ruled_out_when: Every `groupId` in the release runtime classpath maps to a domain the maintainer demonstrably still controls, **and** `verification-metadata.xml` pins a trusted key or checksum for each. Print your counts — an under-counted loop here reads as a clean result (D02-069).

items.title: Duplicate-class shadowing (Maven-Hijack) in the release classpath
items.severity_note: High when the shadowed class is security-relevant (a verifier, a signer, a crypto helper)
items.vrt: `using_components_with_known_vulnerabilities` (varies); `cryptographic_weakness.insufficient_verification_of_data_authenticity.cryptographic_signature` (varies) when the shadowed class is a verifier
items.applies_to: All Gradle/JVM builds
items.maps_to: Gradle blog "Detecting Maven-Hijack-style risks in Gradle builds with the Dependency Analysis Gradle Plugin" — DAGP 3.5.0+, `buildHealth` / `reason` / `fixDependencies`, three risk categories (no duplicates / identical duplicates / incompatible duplicates)
items.skip_when: `test -d "$E/repo" && echo SOURCE=yes || echo SOURCE=no` prints `SOURCE=no` (no source handover; docs/11 §4 has no tag for source access yet) — write `n/a — black-box engagement, no source handover (engagement.json: handover=apk)`.
items.test: Two dependencies both provide the same fully-qualified class; the classloader takes the first on the classpath. An attacker who controls an *earlier* dependency shadows a class belonging to a *later*, trusted one without touching app code.
items.proof: A `buildHealth` entry flagging **binary-incompatible** duplicate classes, e.g. `Expected METHOD com/example/trusty/TrustyService.greet(Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;, but was com/example/trusty/TrustyService.greet(Ljava/lang/String;)I`. Identical duplicates are merely redundant; **incompatible duplicates are the attack signal**.
items.escalation: Combine with D02-055 — hijack the *earlier* `groupId`, ship the shadowing class, done.
items.ruled_out_when: `buildHealth` reports no duplicates, or only identical duplicates, across the release runtime classpath.

items.title: Gradle wrapper jar and distribution URL integrity
items.severity_note: Medium standalone; High when the distribution is fetched over HTTP or from a mutable internal mirror
items.vrt: `insecure_data_transport.executable_download.no_secure_integrity_check` (P4)
items.attacker: AM-06 (MitM on the build host's network) / AM-08
items.applies_to: All Gradle projects
items.maps_to: Gradle "Protecting Project Integrity" (wrapper checksum validation, `distributionSha256Sum` in `gradle-wrapper.properties`, `gradle :wrapper` regeneration from a known-good local distribution); spght.dev (same, plus homoglyph attacks on wrapper scripts)
items.skip_when: `test -d "$E/repo" && echo SOURCE=yes || echo SOURCE=no` prints `SOURCE=no` (no source handover; docs/11 §4 has no tag for source access yet) — write `n/a — black-box engagement, no source handover (engagement.json: handover=apk)`.
items.test: `gradle-wrapper.jar` executes on every build with full developer and CI privileges and is committed as a binary blob. A swapped wrapper jar or an unpinned distribution URL is arbitrary code execution in the build.
items.how:
```bash
shasum -a 256 gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar     # compare against Gradle's published checksums
grep -n 'distributionUrl\|distributionSha256Sum' gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties
gradle wrapper --gradle-version=8.7 --gradle-distribution-sha256-sum=<published-sha256>
```
items.proof: A missing `distributionSha256Sum`, or a `gradle-wrapper.jar` whose SHA-256 matches no published Gradle release checksum. Also flag a `distributionUrl` that is `http://` or points at a non-`services.gradle.org` host.
items.escalation: Build-host RCE -> signing-key theft -> a malicious release signed with the client's real key. Same terminal impact as D02-055; file them as one chain with separate primitives (D02-071).
items.ruled_out_when: The wrapper jar hash matches a published Gradle release, `distributionSha256Sum` is present and correct, and `distributionUrl` is an `https://services.gradle.org` URL.

items.title: Dependencies fetched over plaintext HTTP
items.severity_note: Medium–High (High when the repository serves build-time-executing artefacts, i.e. plugins)
items.vrt: `insecure_data_transport.executable_download.no_secure_integrity_check` (P4)
items.attacker: AM-06 network attacker on the developer's or CI runner's network
items.applies_to: All Gradle builds. Gradle 7+ requires `allowInsecureProtocol = true` to permit an `http://` repository — its presence is an explicit decision.
items.maps_to: GHSA-j6wc-xfg8-jx2j impact section ("Man-in-the-middle attacks: HTTP-based downloads remain vulnerable to interception and replacement")
items.skip_when: `test -d "$E/repo" && echo SOURCE=yes || echo SOURCE=no` prints `SOURCE=no` (no source handover; docs/11 §4 has no tag for source access yet) — write `n/a — black-box engagement, no source handover (engagement.json: handover=apk)`.
items.test: An `http://` Maven repository means every artefact — including ones that execute during the build — is MitM-able.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE "maven[^\n]*\{[^}]*url[^}]*['\"]http://" --include='*.gradle' --include='*.gradle.kts' .
grep -rn "allowInsecureProtocol\|isAllowInsecureProtocol" --include='*.gradle*' .
```
items.proof: The literal repository declaration with an `http://` URL, plus — where you can run the build on a network you control — a proxy log showing the `.jar`/`.aar`/`.pom` fetched in cleartext.
items.escalation: An intercepted plugin jar is build RCE (-> D02-057); an intercepted AAR is a backdoored shipped app (-> D17).
items.ruled_out_when: Every declared repository uses `https://`, and no `allowInsecureProtocol` appears anywhere in the build scripts including `settings.gradle` and `buildSrc`.

items.title: SBOM of the shipped binary, reconciled against the declared graph
items.severity_note: Medium (when the binary contains a component absent from the declared graph)
items.vrt: `using_components_with_known_vulnerabilities` (varies)
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: MASTG-TEST-0274 (SBOM route), MASTG-TECH-0130, MASTG-TOOL-0134 (cdxgen), MASTG-TOOL-0130 (blint); safeguard.sh mobile SBOM guide; susatest ("The final artifact you ship is a binary, not a lockfile. Monitor the binary.")
items.test: Prove the SBOM describes the artefact that reaches users. Scanning a lockfile proves nothing about a DEX plus ARM64 binary.
items.how:
```bash
# source-side (authoritative for coordinates)
./gradlew :app:cyclonedxBom
./gradlew :app:dependencies --configuration releaseRuntimeClasspath > deps.txt
# binary-side (authoritative for what shipped)
syft base.apk -o cyclonedx-json=apk-sbom.json
cdxgen -t android -o apk-sbom.json .
```
Then reconcile: every coordinate in the source SBOM must have a matching class or `.so` in the APK, and vice versa.
items.proof: A reconciliation table with a non-empty "in source SBOM but not in APK" column (dead weight -> lower severity on any CVE there) and a non-empty "in APK but not in source SBOM" column (vendored/shaded code, a jar in `assets/`, a plugin-injected library -> a supply-chain finding in its own right).
items.escalation: Feeds D02-060 (osv-scanner) and D02-008 (source-to-artefact correspondence). An undeclared bundled component is a reportable control failure even before any CVE.
items.ruled_out_when: Both columns of the reconciliation are empty. A source-only SBOM never rules this out — the whole point is the binary side.
